title: The Escape of the Pandavas
body:
The Escape of the Pandavas

न बिभेति कदाचित्तु धर्मे तिष्ठति यो नरः।
ईश्वरस्तस्य रक्षकः सङ्कटेऽपि महत्यपि॥

"A person who stands firmly upon the path of righteousness never experiences fear. The Supreme Lord remains his protector, even in the midst of the gravest calamities."

As the Pandavas prepared to depart Hastinapur, Vidura stepped forward to bid them farewell. Speaking in a cryptic, mlecchha-bhasha dialect understood only by Yudhishthira, he gave a veiled warning: 'He alone will escape who forestalls the intentions of an astute enemy. The conflagration that devastates a forest cannot hurt a rat which shelters itself in a hole or a porcupine which burrows in the earth. The wise man knows his bearings by looking at the stars.' Upon reaching Varanavata, Yudhishthira kept his brothers alert, confirming that the palace indeed smelled of ghee, lac, and fat.
Soon, an expert miner sent in secret by Vidura arrived at the palace, offering his services with the passcode: 'The forest fire cannot hurt the burrowing rat.' Working in absolute secrecy for many weeks, the miner excavated a deep, secure subterranean egress that ran right beneath the clay walls and the surrounding moat, opening into the safety of the distant forest. On the fated night, knowing Purochana intended to light the fire, the Pandavas preempted him. Setting fire to Purochana's own quarters and the highly inflammable corners of the palace, they entered the tunnel, escaping into the pitch-black night just as the wax palace erupted into a towering column of flames.
They emerged into the deep, wild forest. As Kunti, Nakula, and Sahadeva collapsed from sheer exhaustion and terror, the giant Bhima carried his mother on his shoulders, his twin brothers on his hips, and supported Yudhishthira and Arjuna with his powerful arms, effortlessly forcing his way through the tangled undergrowth. They crossed the fast-flowing Ganges in a boat provided by Vidura's loyal boatman, entering the dense forest of Ekachakra disguised as humble Brahmanas. On their way, they met Sage Vyasa, who consoled Kunti: 'Life is a tangled web of good and evil; no virtuous man is entirely free from sorrow, nor is any sinner exempt from consequence. Put on the garb of Brahmanas, and bide your time in Ekachakra.' This escape is a beautiful allegory of the Jivatma's escape from the fiery trap of material attachments through the inner conduit of discrimination (Viveka) and the guidance of a spiritual mentor.
